Quantitative Sociologist · Survey Methodologist

Jiayun Jin

My research sits at the intersection of quantitative sociology and survey methodology. On the substantive side, I am interested in gender, work, and social attitudes; on the methodological side, I study measurement quality, survey inference, and the relationship between observed data and the phenomena they are intended to represent.

What connects these strands is a shared concern with the gap between observed data and the social phenomena they are meant to represent: are we observing what we think we are observing?

01 / About

I am a quantitative sociologist and survey methodologist studying gender inequality in work, attitudes, and well-being. I use large-scale cross-national and panel surveys to examine how organisational arrangements, social expectations, and family circumstances shape unequal experiences of work. My methodological research on survey measurement and inference complements this substantive programme by asking how reliably those inequalities are captured in empirical data.

My research programme brings together two strands of expertise. In substantive sociology, I study gender attitudes and the organisation of work, including how working from home, schedule control, and access to short-notice time off relate to work–family conflict and well-being. In survey methodology, my guiding question has stayed the same since my PhD: are we observing what we think we are observing? My doctoral research at KU Leuven developed statistical approaches for detecting measurement error during data collection; this work later received the Innovation Prize at the Netherlands Platform for Survey Research. I continue to use latent-variable, mixture, multilevel, longitudinal, weighting, and simulation methods to study both substantive inequality and the quality of the evidence used to describe it.

I am currently based in the Netherlands, developing research on gender, flexible work, well-being, panel representativeness, and survey inference. I am particularly interested in research environments where rigorous quantitative analysis can contribute to substantive debates and practical questions about equality and the organisation of work.

02 / Research

Research Areas

My research combines substantive questions about gender, work, and well-being with rigorous analysis of survey and panel data. A parallel methodological strand examines measurement quality, representativeness, and statistical adjustment in complex social data.

Gender, Work & Well-being

Gender differences in flexible working, schedule control, work–family conflict, well-being, and attitudes, with particular interest in when workplace flexibility increases autonomy and when it reproduces unequal constraints.

Survey & Panel Research

Longitudinal and cross-sectional survey analysis, attrition and representativeness, harmonisation across waves, weighting, external benchmarking, and data-quality monitoring.

Quantitative Social Research

Multilevel modelling, longitudinal analysis, latent-variable and mixture models, complex-survey methods, and simulation-based evaluation for substantive social-science questions.

Measurement & Data Quality

Questionnaire-based measurement, response behaviour, measurement error, statistical monitoring, and the interpretation of indicators used in large-scale social research.

Survey Inference & Adjustment

Calibration weighting, inverse probability weighting, mass imputation, doubly robust estimators, and the role of auxiliary information in non-probability survey inference.

Reproducible & Computational Workflows

R- and Python-based workflows that make data processing, modelling choices, text coding, and measurement decisions transparent, auditable, and reproducible.

04 / Projects

Current Research Projects

Gender, Flexible Work and Well-being in the 2024 EWCS

Working from home, schedule control, work–family conflict and well-being across 35 countries
R EWCS 2024 Gender & Work-Family Multilevel Modelling
What it does

An exploratory analysis of the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey (n = 36,644; 35 countries) examining gender differences across distinct dimensions of workplace flexibility, including working-from-home frequency, schedule control, and the ability to take short-notice time off. Multilevel models with country random intercepts examine whether associations of working from home with work–family conflict and well-being vary by gender and schedule control.

Current research extending my work on gender inequality to the organisation of work, asking when flexible working increases autonomy and when it instead reflects adaptation to unequal work and care demands.
Schedule control, ease of time off, and working from home, by gender and caregiving status
Women report somewhat more working from home than men, but lower schedule control (≈35% vs. ≈40–44%); the ability to arrange short-notice time off is more similar across genders.
See more (work–family conflict and well-being, by WFH frequency, schedule control, and gender)
Work–family conflict by WFH frequency, schedule control, and gender
Conflict rises more steeply with WFH frequency under low schedule control, particularly for women. The pattern is descriptive: the corresponding three-way interaction (WFH frequency × schedule control × gender) is not statistically significant (p = .17).
Predicted well-being (WHO-5), by WFH frequency, schedule control, and gender
Among respondents with low schedule control, predicted well-being rises with WFH frequency for men but declines slightly for women. Here the three-way interaction (WFH frequency × schedule control × gender) is statistically significant (p = .041).

LISS Panel Quality & Representativeness

Reproducible monitoring of panel composition and participation
View on GitHub ↗
R Panel Representativeness Data Quality Audit Longitudinal Monitoring
What it does

A reproducible monitoring workflow for the LISS panel (Longitudinal Internet Studies for the Social Sciences), built on the monthly LISS Background Variables. Audits the underlying monthly files for schema and data-quality consistency across waves, and compares the panel's age and sex composition against CBS population benchmarks — separately for the full eligible panel and for participating members.

Early-stage: the background-file audit, representativeness monitoring, and participation/attrition monitoring (a doetmee-pattern classification, exit definition, retention curve, and discrete-time hazard model of panel exit) are implemented; a weighting demonstration linked to nonprob-survey-inference is planned next.
Retention curve (starting cohort), by age
The same starting cohort, tracked over time, splits the same two age groups worst off for different reasons: 25–34 mostly leaves the panel file entirely, while 15–24 mostly goes quiet while still enrolled (“soft” attrition) — a distinction the exit-rate figure alone can't show.
See more (representativeness gap, exit rates by group)
Age representation vs. CBS benchmark
Younger age groups (16–24, 25–34) are underrepresented, and the gap widens further among participating members; older groups (55+) are overrepresented, most sharply at 65+.
Exit rate by baseline demographic group
Recruitment cohort shows by far the largest gap: members recruited in 2023/24 exit at roughly 2.6× the rate of established (pre-2023) members (47.4% vs. 18.0%), consistent with attrition concentrating in the first years after joining.

Non-Probability Survey Inference

R simulation workflow for survey inference under selection bias
View on GitHub ↗

An R-based methodological project comparing calibration weighting, inverse probability weighting, mass imputation, and doubly robust estimation under different selection mechanisms and auxiliary-information conditions. The project asks a conditional question rather than seeking a single “best” method: when do adjustment methods work, and when do their assumptions break down?

Main finding: results are conditional
Ignorable selection
Non-ignorable selection
Strong auxiliary variables
✓ Works well
~ Partial reduction
Weak auxiliary variables
~ Marginal gain
✗ Breaks down
Takeaway: there is no universally best method — performance depends on the selection mechanism and the quality of auxiliary information.
Beyond binary: a continuous non-ignorability gradient
A follow-up round replaces the binary ignorable / non-ignorable comparison with a continuous parameter (γ) controlling how strongly selection depends on the outcome. Once γ > 0, calibration, IPW, and doubly robust estimation become close substitutes — their differences are small relative to the bias γ introduces. What matters is whether the auxiliary variables can proxy for that outcome-dependence: strong auxiliary information absorbs part of the bias, while weak auxiliary information offers little protection.
See preliminary results (γ-sweep chart)
Methodological Side Project

OpenCodebook

A Python framework for transparent, auditable, model-assisted coding of open-ended survey responses. Researchers define structured codebooks in YAML; local open-source models apply the codes; the pipeline produces structured outputs with reliability diagnostics and reviewable audit trails. The project complements my empirical research by exploring reproducible ways to incorporate open-ended survey data without losing interpretability or auditability.

Gender Attitude Latent Structures

Research on hidden heterogeneity in gender attitude surveys using mixture models and latent-class analysis. Published in Sociological Methods & Research (2025). Currently extending to open-ended text responses.

Fig. 1 — A response-process model for Likert-scale answers
Fig. 4 — Latent profile membership by gender and education
From Jin (2025), Disentangling and Reassembling: Unveiling Hidden Patterns in Gender Attitudinal Surveys, Sociological Methods & Research. A multi-process response model separates non-substantive, midpoint, and extreme response tendencies from underlying gender attitudes, identifying five latent profiles whose prevalence varies systematically by gender and education.
